activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can explain how covalent bonds form and name covalent compounds.

**Think of splitting a pizza.** Nobody gives the pizza away; you both eat from it. A **covalent bond** works the same way. Two **nonmetal** atoms both need more electrons, and neither will give any up, so they **share**.

**How the bond forms.** Each atom puts in one electron to make a **shared pair**. The shared pair counts toward the outer level of **both** atoms, so both can reach a full outer level (8 for most atoms, 2 for hydrogen). No electrons are given away, so **no ions form**. A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds is a **molecule**.

**How many bonds?** An atom shares as many electrons as it needs to fill its outer level (8, or 2 for hydrogen). Hydrogen needs 1 (1 bond). Group 17 needs 1 (1 bond). Group 16 needs 2 (2 bonds). Group 15 needs 3 (3 bonds). Group 14 needs 4 (4 bonds).

**Single, double, triple.** A **single bond** is 1 shared pair (2 electrons). A **double bond** is 2 shared pairs (4 electrons). A **triple bond** is 3 shared pairs (6 electrons).

**Naming covalent compounds.** Use **prefixes** to count the atoms: mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6, hepta 7, octa 8, nona 9, deca 10. The **first element skips mono**. The **second element always gets a prefix** and an **-ide** ending. Drop the extra o or a before oxide (monoxide, tetroxide, pentoxide). No criss-cross and no reducing: the prefixes are the subscripts.

**Worked example 1:** How does water form? Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more. Each hydrogen needs 1 more. So oxygen shares one pair with each of two hydrogens: H₂O, with two single bonds.

**Worked example 2:** Why does N₂ have a triple bond? Each nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more, so the two atoms share 3 pairs.

**Worked example 3:** Name N₂O₅. Both are nonmetals, so use prefixes. 2 nitrogens → dinitrogen; 5 oxygens → pentoxide. Answer: **dinitrogen pentoxide**. And sulfur trioxide is 1 sulfur and 3 oxygens: **SO₃**.

**Watch out for:** saying electrons are transferred (that is ionic), saying the atoms become ions, counting a single bond as 1 electron instead of 2, putting mono on the first element, leaving the prefixes out ("phosphorus chloride"), reducing a covalent formula (N₂O₄ is not NO₂), and using Roman numerals on nonmetals.
prompts: Explain how two chlorine atoms form a covalent bond in Cl₂. Say what the electrons do and how each atom ends up with 8.
Oxygen gas is O₂ and nitrogen gas is N₂. Explain why O₂ has a double bond but N₂ has a triple bond.
Name these compounds and explain your thinking for each: CO, PCl₃, and N₂O₄.
Write the formulas for sulfur hexafluoride and dinitrogen trioxide. Explain how the prefixes gave you the subscripts.
